---
title: "Zotero integration"
subtitle: "Keep adding papers in Zotero — new references and their PDFs flow into FluxLib automatically"
---

If you already live in Zotero — or your papers arrive through its excellent browser
connector — you don't have to choose between Zotero and Flux. Connect them once and
Zotero becomes an intake valve for [FluxLib](../concepts/library-and-fluxlib.qmd): anything
you add there appears in Flux, with its PDF, ready to read, annotate, cite, and search.

# What it does — and what it never does

The connection is **one-way and additive**. On every sync, Flux reads a Zotero *export
file* (set up below) and brings in whatever FluxLib doesn't already have. That's the whole
contract. Concretely:

- **New Zotero references are added** to FluxLib, keeping their Better BibTeX citation keys.
- **Their PDFs come along** — copied into FluxLib or linked in place, your choice (see
  [PDFs: copied or linked](#pdfs-copied-or-linked)).
- **Papers you already have are recognized and left alone.** Matching is by DOI first, then
  by title + author + year for entries without one. Your existing citekeys, PDFs, notes, and
  annotations are never touched.
- **Nothing is ever written back to Zotero.** Flux never modifies your Zotero library, its
  database, or its files.
- **Deleting or editing in Zotero changes nothing in Flux.** FluxLib is your permanent
  collection; Zotero is just one of the doors into it.

Syncing is safe to run any number of times — a second sync of the same export is a no-op.

# One-time setup in Zotero

Flux reads a **Better BibTeX auto-export**: a `.bib` file that Zotero keeps rewriting on its
own whenever your library changes. Setting that up takes two minutes:

1. **Install the Better BibTeX plugin** (free, open source). Download the `.xpi` from
   [retorque.re/zotero-better-bibtex](https://retorque.re/zotero-better-bibtex/) and in
   Zotero choose **Tools → Plugins → gear menu → Install Plugin From File…**, then restart
   Zotero.
2. **Create the auto-export.** Right-click your library (or a single collection — see
   [Very large libraries](#very-large-libraries)) and choose **Export Library…**. Set the
   format to **Better BibTeX**, and tick **Keep updated** — this is the crucial checkbox.
   Save the `.bib` file anywhere you like; next to your Zotero data folder is a fine choice.

From now on, Better BibTeX silently rewrites that file every time your Zotero library
changes. That file is the entire interface between the two apps — Flux never talks to
Zotero itself, so nothing here depends on Zotero being open.

# Connecting Flux

In [Library](../modes/library.qmd), click the **Zotero** button in the header and point
Flux at the export:

- **Choose .bib…** — the auto-export file you just created.
- **Zotero folder…** — your Zotero data folder (usually `~/Zotero`; its `storage` subfolder
  holds the PDFs). Flux needs this to find PDFs that the export references by relative
  path. If you skip it, PDFs stored with absolute paths still work.
- **Copy vs. link** — how PDFs are brought in; see the next section.
- **Sync automatically** — on by default: Flux syncs at startup and live while the app is
  open. Turn it off if you'd rather sync only from the button.

Click **Connect & sync** and the first sync runs immediately. A toast reports what happened
("12 added · 3 already known · 9 PDFs copied"). The button in the Library header shows
**Zotero ✓** while connected; click it any time for status, **Sync now**, settings, or
**Disconnect**.

# When syncs happen

- **At startup**, quietly, shortly after the app opens (it never delays launch).
- **Live**, while Flux is open: when Zotero changes your library, Better BibTeX rewrites
  the export, and Flux notices within a couple of seconds.
- **On demand**, from **Sync now** in the Zotero panel.

Automatic syncs cost essentially nothing when there's nothing to do: Flux checks the export
file's timestamp and size first, and if they haven't changed since the last successful
sync, it skips all work — no reading, no parsing, no toast. **Sync now** is different: it
always performs a complete pass, which also picks up PDFs that appeared in Zotero's folder
*after* their reference was synced (see below).

# PDFs: copied or linked

When a synced reference declares a PDF, Flux brings it in one of two ways — chosen at
connect time, changeable later under **Settings…**:

- **Copy PDFs into FluxLib** (the default). The PDF is stored in FluxLib itself, so your
  FluxLib folder remains a complete, self-contained archive — back it up or move it to a
  new machine and every paper comes along. Recommended for most libraries: the one-time
  disk cost of a typical collection is a few gigabytes.
- **Link to Zotero's PDFs.** Flux stores only a small pointer to the PDF where it already
  lives in Zotero's folder — one copy on disk, no duplication. The tradeoff: Zotero's
  folder must stay where it is. If a linked file is later moved or deleted, that paper
  simply shows as having no PDF (nothing else breaks), and a **Sync now** re-links it if
  it reappears.

Either way, Flux extracts the paper's text so [full-text search](../modes/library.qmd#finding-papers)
(`ft:`) covers it — unless you deferred that (next section).

Two behaviors worth knowing:

- **Late PDFs are backfilled.** If a reference synced before its PDF existed (say, Zotero
  grabbed the metadata but the PDF download came later), the next sync attaches the PDF to
  the existing entry. Existing PDFs are never replaced.
- **PDFs Flux fetched itself always win.** A stored PDF in FluxLib is never displaced by a
  Zotero copy or pointer.

# Very large libraries

If you connect a huge export (thousands of references), the connect dialog notices the file
size and preselects the sensible posture automatically: **link** mode, with **Extract
searchable text during sync** turned off. In that configuration the sync never opens a
single PDF — it just records where each one lives — so even a first sync of a 15,000-PDF
library finishes in seconds rather than grinding through every file. This matters doubly
when Zotero's folder lives on a cloud drive (Google Drive, Dropbox), where reading every
PDF once would mean streaming your entire collection over the network.

With text extraction deferred, a paper becomes full-text-searchable after the first time
you open it in the [Reader](../modes/reader.qmd) (Flux extracts and caches the text
quietly at that moment). Until then it's still findable by title, author, abstract, and
all other metadata.

Two tips for the truly gigantic:

- **Export a collection, not the whole library.** Better BibTeX itself slows down keeping
  a 30,000-entry export current — it rewrites the entire file on every change. Right-click
  a *collection* and auto-export that instead; the sync is additive, so you lose nothing
  by starting focused.
- Keep only the PDFs on the cloud drive — Zotero's own database (`zotero.sqlite`) on a
  synced folder is a well-known source of corruption. That's Zotero advice, not Flux
  advice, but it protects the files your links point at.

# Fitting into a library you already have

Connecting Zotero to an established FluxLib is seamless — the first sync just recognizes
everything you already have (by DOI, or title + author + year) and skips it. The only
cosmetic effect: new arrivals keep their Better BibTeX citation keys, which is also the
exact format Flux itself generates (`smithNeuralBasis2021`-style), so keys look uniform
regardless of which door a paper came through. The rare duplicate — the same paper with no
DOI *and* meaningfully different metadata in the two places, like a preprint versus its
published version — comes in as a second entry; delete whichever you don't want.

# Capturing papers from your browser

Once connected, the [Zotero Connector](https://www.zotero.org/download/connectors) browser
extension becomes the best way to capture papers from the web: one click on any paper page
saves it to Zotero — with publisher-quality metadata and, where possible, the PDF — and it
flows into FluxLib on the next sync. This works alongside Flux's own
[web capture](web-capture.qmd) and add-by-DOI box; use whichever is
in reach.

# Syncing from the command line (and agents)

The same sync runs headlessly as `flux zotero-sync` — useful in scripts, cron jobs, and
for AI agents keeping your library current. Like automatic syncs, it skips an unchanged
export; `--force` performs a complete pass. See the [command-line reference](../reference/cli.qmd)
for all flags.

# Disconnecting

**Disconnect** in the Zotero panel forgets the connection settings — nothing else.
Everything already synced stays in FluxLib exactly as it is. (If you used **link** mode,
those papers' PDFs still live in Zotero's folder, so keep it around or re-sync in copy
mode first.)

# Troubleshooting

- **"PDFs not found" in the sync toast.** The export references PDFs by paths Flux
  couldn't resolve — usually the **Zotero folder** setting is missing or points to the
  wrong place. Open the Zotero panel → **Settings…** and point it at the folder whose
  `storage` subfolder holds the PDFs, then **Sync now**.
- **A linked paper won't open.** Its file moved — most often because Zotero's folder was
  relocated or a cloud drive is offline. Restore the folder (or reconnect and **Sync now**
  to re-link), or switch to copy mode if this keeps happening.
- **Full-text search doesn't find a paper you know is there.** If you deferred text
  extraction (large-library setup), the paper's text is indexed after you first open it in
  the Reader. Open it once, or run a sync with text extraction enabled.
- **New Zotero papers aren't appearing.** Check that the auto-export still exists and has
  **Keep updated** ticked (in Zotero: **Edit → Settings → Better BibTeX → Automatic
  export**, or right-click the export entry under the collection). Then **Sync now** —
  its toast will tell you what it found.
- **The same paper appears twice.** It lacked a DOI and its metadata differed between
  Zotero and FluxLib (common with preprints). Delete the copy you don't want; the sync
  won't re-add it as long as the survivor matches by DOI or title + author + year.
